desc:
A number triangle is given as a list of rows: row i has exactly i + 1 positive integers. A descent starts at the single number in the top row and moves down one row at a time. From position j in row i it may go to position j or position j + 1 in row i + 1.

A descent is valid only if any two consecutive numbers on it have different parity (one is even and the other is odd). Return the largest sum of a valid descent from the top row to the bottom row, or -1 if no valid descent exists.
hints: Without the parity rule this is the classic triangle maximum path. Which part of the state do you need to add to enforce the rule, and is that already part of the state?

The parity of the current number is determined by the cell itself, so the cell position alone is enough. Define down[i][j] as the best valid sum from cell (i, j) to the bottom, or -1 if there is none.

Work from the bottom row up: the last row has down = value. For a cell, look only at the two children whose value has the opposite parity and whose down is not -1; take the larger one and add the cell's value. If no child qualifies, down is -1.
editorial: The validity of a step depends only on the two numbers it connects, and both are known once the cell positions are known. So no extra dimension is needed: the sub-problem 'best valid descent from cell (i, j) to the bottom' is self-contained, because the rule for later steps depends only on the parity of cell (i, j), which is fixed.

Bottom-up: in the last row every cell is its own descent. For other cells down[i][j] = value + max(down[child]), where only children with the opposite parity and a valid descent are allowed. Since all numbers are positive, a real sum is never negative and -1 is a safe marker for 'impossible'. If the top cell gets -1 there is no valid descent at all (for example when all numbers have the same parity and the triangle has more than one row). Time O(n2), space O(n).
